{"category":"convention","name":"Per-design state never lives in a process-global, and identity is an id that resolves to a location — never a path","statement":"TWO CLAUSES, ONE PURPOSE: keep reflow2 able to hold many designs in one process without a rewrite.

(1) STATE THAT BELONGS TO A DESIGN LIVES ON THE DESIGN HANDLE, NOT IN A `static`. cap:graph-registry already names the ones that must move — graph_path, content_path, identity, and the write_gen counter the loop nudge reads — and every new process-global that is secretly per-design adds another line to that migration. Legitimately process-wide state is fine and exists today (the seat registry, the serve-shared mode flag); the test is not 'is it a static' but 'would this need a different value for a second design open in the same process'.

(2) A DESIGN IS NAMED BY AN ID THAT RESOLVES TO A LOCATION. cap:select-graph-by-id frames it correctly — the server maps id to path — so the id is primary and the path is a storage detail. A surface that treats a filesystem path as the canonical identity forecloses object storage, where the location is a key and the identity rides as metadata.

WHY THIS IS A RULE RATHER THAN A REQUIREMENT: it constrains HOW every other change is made rather than describing behaviour anything can satisfy — the same shape as rule:no-foreclosure and rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party.

EVIDENCE, 2026-08-09, from Anthony's question about running reflow2 behind a web app at 1k / 100k / 1M tenants (dec:idea-a-hosted-tier-of-many-single-writer-tenants). Neither clause costs anything today; both are expensive to retrofit, and the failure mode is erosion rather than a decision — one convenient global at a time, invisible until the migration. reflow2's own design measured 1,828 nodes = 3.8 MB export vs 33 MB store, which is what makes hold-many-designs-per-process the architecture rather than an option.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY: nothing about WHERE a design is stored, nothing about hosting, and nothing that requires the registry to be built. It only keeps the door open."}
